extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, employers, policymakers, economists, and commenters participating in FTC rulemaking on employee non-compete agreements
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the legal, procedural, and empirical standards the Commission used in the final rule and regulatory analysis concerning non-compete agreements, including definitions, data choices, modeling decisions, and statutory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance period (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission refers to the period between the publication of the final rule and the date on which compliance with the final rule is required as the 'compliance period.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines an implementation timing term used throughout the rule and regulatory analysis (see id. at 3515).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on effective date imposed by the CRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments did not consider the limitations on the effective date imposed by the CRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Congressional Review Act constrains how and when an agency can set an effective date; rule writers and commenters must account for CRA-imposed limits when proposing or evaluating effective dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rescission requirement (Commission decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is not finalizing a rescission requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in Part IV.E; indicates the Commission decided not to require employers to rescind previously entered non-competes as part of the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure-only rule for senior executives insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considered whether a disclosure rule would be appropriate for senior executives, but concludes that it is not because it would fail to address many of the ways in which non-competes are restrictive and exclusionary and tend to negatively affect competitive conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies a substantive criterion: disclosure-only approaches do not remedy the competitive harms the Commission identifies and therefore are inadequate as a regulatory response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchise Rule disclosure and prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Franchise Rule requires franchisors to disclose any non-compete that franchisees must impose on managers. These non-competes are prohibited by the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references Parts III.D and V.D.6; signals that non-competes imposed on franchise managers, though previously disclosable, are barred under the final FTC rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance/guidelines not a viable alternative to a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: By definition, a guidance document would 'not have the force and effect of law.' Guidelines would not bind employers or courts and would not provide workers with the same clarity about the enforceability of their non-competes. The Commission finds that the issuance of guidelines is not a viable alternative to the final rule for the same reasons that it finds that the no-action alternative generally is not a viable alternative to the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal precedent cited (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass'n, Shalala v. Guernsey Mem'l Hosp.) supports the proposition that guidance cannot substitute for rulemaking when binding clarity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-law occupational limits on non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: In most States, those limits apply to just one or two occupations (most commonly, physicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that existing state restrictions are often narrow in scope; important context when assessing national rule impacts and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-of-law clauses: typical deference and statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, courts defer to choice of law clauses because they are presumed to represent the express intention of the parties. Some States have enacted statutes banning selection of a different State's law for a non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: while choice-of-law provisions are normally honored, agency and counsel should be aware of recent state statutes (e.g., California, Minnesota, Colorado, Massachusetts, Louisiana) that restrict or ban choice-of-law selection for non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and scaling of non-compete enforceability scores (0–1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different researchers have rescaled this score in different ways (e.g., from zero to 470, or scaled such that the mean score is zero and the standard deviation of the score is one). The Commission uses the scaling from zero to one because that is the way it is used in the majority of the studies which are relied on in the final analysis, as well as for easy interpretability and consistency across the final analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological choice: adopt 0–1 scaling for consistency with the literature used in the analysis; when replicating or critiquing the analysis, ensure comparable scaling or adjust estimates accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of average magnitude change (0.081) as a scaling reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considers a change whose magnitude is equal to the average of the magnitudes of all those changes. See Johnson, Lavetti, & Lipsitz for details; the Commission uses the average magnitude change of 0.081 to scale effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This averaged change supplements full extrapolation methods; the Commission notes limitations of using this average and uses conservative approaches and sensitivity analysis (and also reports full extrapolation results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical modelling formulas for percent effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission reports and uses exponential transformation formulas to translate coefficients into percent effects, e.g., calculated as −(e^(−0.107*0.081) − 1) for earnings, e^(1.43*0.06) − 1 and e^(2.56*0.06) − 1 for patenting effects, and e^(0.427*0.081) − 1 for physician prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling practice: apply reported coefficient estimates from cited studies using exponential transforms to compute percentage changes; document coefficient sources and the Δ enforceability values used in calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of States with broadly non-enforceable non-competes from certain estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Earnings from California, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and Minnesota (States which broadly do not enforce non-competes) are subtracted out, since enforceability in those States will be broadly unaffected by the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State inclusion/exclusion materially affects national aggregates; analysts should follow the Commission's approach or explicitly justify alternative treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Fitzpatrick Matrix as a proxy for litigation counsel rates (conservative)
rubrics_metrics.description: This estimate is drawn from the Fitzpatrick Matrix, which is a fee schedule used by many U.S. courts for determining the reasonable hourly rates in the District of Columbia for attorneys' fee awards under Federal fee-shifting statutes. It is used here as a proxy for market rates for litigation counsel in the Washington, DC area...The estimate is therefore adjusted to reflect a national rate...The Commission conservatively uses the rates of a tenth-year attorney—a much more experienced attorney than is likely to be needed (and indeed no attorney at all may be needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating litigation costs, the Commission favors conservative (higher) assumptions and explains adjustments (DC->national wage ratio, selection of years of experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's approach to conservative parameter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission uses the low end of the reported range in order to exercise caution against extrapolation...The Commission conservatively uses certain assumptions (e.g., tenth-year attorney rates) and notes where supplementary methods are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical principle: prefer conservative (cautious) parameter choices and explicitly state when low-end estimates are used to avoid overstating impacts; include sensitivity analyses and alternative extrapolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirement: Commission not required to analyze costs/benefits of regulatory alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is not required to analyze costs and benefits of regulatory alternatives in its final regulatory analysis. See 15 U.S.C. 57b-3(b)(2)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural/legal standard limiting what the final regulatory analysis must contain with respect to alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of transfers versus benefits in welfare accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission notes that this analysis does not measure or consider whether earnings are transfers or benefits because to the extent that the earnings that are transfers represent firms' ability to suppress earnings using an unfair method of competition, the transfer of such earnings from firms to workers through the use of non-competes still reflect the tendency of non-competes to negatively affect competitive conditions in the labor market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual rule: the Commission treats certain transfers (from firms to workers) arising from correcting unfair competitive conduct as reflecting improvements in competitive conditions rather than excluding them as mere transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-specific estimation method for covered workers and earnings impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: For illustrative purposes, State-specific estimates are displayed in Appendix Table A.1. In this table, the estimated number of covered workers is calculated as 80% * (total employed population in the State); the estimated increase in total earnings is calculated as 0.86% * (estimated total covered earnings), where estimated total covered earnings is calculated as (estimated number of covered workers) * (average annual earnings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides explicit per-state calculation steps and data sources (Census/BLS) for reproducing state-level impacts; highlights the 80% coverage assumption and the percentage effect (0.86%) used in that illustrative computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of mixed empirical evidence and methodological caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence in the empirical literature is mixed. Some studies find increases in firm value when non-competes became enforceable in Michigan; other studies find no effect on firm value when non-competes were prohibited for the majority of workers in Washington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts and commenters should recognize heterogeneity in empirical findings and the limits of extrapolation across contexts; the Commission incorporates such nuance into sensitivity and robustness discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: churn
rubrics_metrics.description: Churn in this context means turnover that is neither job creation nor job destruction—essentially the movement of workers among jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies terminology used in labor-market impact discussion and economic modelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data provenance requirement and explicit citation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission documents the specific data sources and study versions used (e.g., enforceability score data come from Starr (2019) reporting scores for 2009; some studies were released after the NPRM and are noted when used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical practice: explicitly identify data vintage, any adjustments (e.g., rescaling), and whether studies were published after the NPRM; transparency about data provenance and timing is required in the regulatory record.
